notes:
1. Mahatma Gandhi — Overview

  • Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi became the principal leader of India's mass national movement from 1919 onward.
  • He transformed Indian nationalism through:
  • Satyagraha.
  • Ahimsa.
  • Non-Cooperation.
  • Civil Disobedience.
  • Constructive work.
  • Mass mobilisation.
  • His political methods drew peasants, workers, women, students and ordinary citizens into the freedom struggle.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi → Satyagraha + Ahimsa + Mass Nationalism

2. Full Name

  • His full name was Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi.
📌 Must-Memorise

M.K. Gandhi → Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi

3. Birth

  • Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869.
  • His birthplace was Porbandar in present-day Gujarat.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi → 2 October 1869 → Porbandar

4. Father

  • Gandhi's father was Karamchand Uttamchand Gandhi.
  • He served as Diwan of Porbandar and later in other princely administrations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Father → Karamchand Gandhi

5. Mother

  • Gandhi's mother was Putlibai.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mother → Putlibai

6. Religious Environment

  • Gandhi grew up in a Vaishnava household.
  • Jain ideas of:
  • Ahimsa.
  • Fasting.
  • Self-discipline.

also influenced the cultural environment of Gujarat.

7. Marriage

  • Gandhi married Kasturba Makhanji in 1883.
  • Both were teenagers at the time.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi's Wife → Kasturba Gandhi

8. Kasturba Gandhi

  • Kasturba became an important participant in:
  • South African struggles.
  • Ashram life.
  • Indian nationalist movements.

9. Education in India

  • Gandhi studied in Gujarat before travelling to England for legal education.

10. England

  • Gandhi went to London in 1888 to study law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi → London → 1888

11. Inner Temple

  • Gandhi joined the Inner Temple, one of London's Inns of Court.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi → Inner Temple

12. Called to the Bar

  • Gandhi qualified as a barrister in 1891.

13. Return to India

  • Gandhi returned to India in 1891.
  • His initial legal career in India was not particularly successful.

14. South Africa

  • Gandhi travelled to South Africa in 1893.
  • He went there in connection with a legal case involving an Indian merchant firm.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi → South Africa → 1893

15. Dada Abdulla

  • Gandhi's South African journey was connected with the business firm of Dada Abdulla and Company.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dada Abdulla → Gandhi's South Africa Legal Assignment

16. Pietermaritzburg Incident

  • In June 1893, Gandhi was removed from a first-class railway compartment at Pietermaritzburg despite possessing a valid ticket.
  • The incident became a major turning point in his political consciousness.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pietermaritzburg → 1893 → Racial Discrimination Against Gandhi

17. Racial Discrimination in South Africa

Indian residents faced:

  • Segregation.
  • Voting restrictions.
  • Registration laws.
  • Movement restrictions.
  • Racial humiliation.

18. Natal Indian Congress

  • Gandhi founded the Natal Indian Congress in 1894.
📌 Must-Memorise

Natal Indian Congress → 1894 → Gandhi

19. Purpose of Natal Indian Congress

It sought to:

  • Organise Indians politically.
  • Petition authorities.
  • Fight racial discrimination.
  • Develop public opinion.

20. Indian Opinion

  • Gandhi started the newspaper Indian Opinion in South Africa in 1903.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Opinion → 1903 → Gandhi

21. Importance of Indian Opinion

  • It became an important medium for:
  • Political education.
  • Communication.
  • Campaigning against discrimination.

22. Phoenix Settlement

  • Gandhi established the Phoenix Settlement near Durban in 1904.
📌 Must-Memorise

Phoenix Settlement → South Africa → Gandhi

23. Ruskin's Influence

  • John Ruskin's Unto This Last deeply influenced Gandhi.
  • Gandhi drew from it ideas concerning:
  • Dignity of labour.
  • Simplicity.
  • Welfare of all.

24. Sarvodaya

  • Gandhi rendered the central message he drew from Ruskin into the concept of Sarvodaya.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sarvodaya → Welfare/Uplift of All

25. Leo Tolstoy

  • Russian writer Leo Tolstoy influenced Gandhi's thinking on:
  • Non-violence.
  • Moral resistance.
  • Simplicity.

26. Tolstoy Farm

  • Gandhi and Hermann Kallenbach established Tolstoy Farm near Johannesburg in 1910.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tolstoy Farm → 1910 → Gandhi + Hermann Kallenbach

27. Henry David Thoreau

  • Gandhi was also influenced by writings on civil disobedience associated with Henry David Thoreau.
  • Gandhi nevertheless developed Satyagraha in his own distinct ethical and political framework.

28. Bhagavad Gita

  • The Bhagavad Gita became one of Gandhi's most important spiritual texts.
  • He interpreted its message primarily in ethical and non-violent terms.

29. Satyagraha

  • Gandhi developed Satyagraha during his South African struggles.
  • The term means broadly:
  • Holding firmly to truth.
  • Truth-force.
📌 Must-Memorise

Satyagraha → Truth-Force

30. Satyagraha vs Passive Resistance

For Gandhi, Satyagraha was not simply passive resistance.

It required:

  • Truth.
  • Non-violence.
  • Self-discipline.
  • Willingness to suffer.
  • Refusal to hate the opponent.

31. First Major Satyagraha Campaign

  • A major organised Satyagraha began in the Transvaal in 1906.
  • It opposed discriminatory registration legislation.
📌 Must-Memorise

South African Satyagraha → 1906

32. Asiatic Registration Act

  • Indians were required to register and carry certificates under discriminatory laws.
  • Gandhi's followers called such legislation the "Black Act."

33. Johannesburg Meeting

  • On 11 September 1906, a mass meeting in Johannesburg pledged resistance to discriminatory registration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

11 September 1906 → Early Organised Satyagraha

34. Burning Registration Certificates

  • Gandhi and his followers publicly burned registration certificates during the struggle.

35. Imprisonment

  • Gandhi was imprisoned several times in South Africa for resistance to discriminatory laws.

36. 1913 South African Campaign

  • In 1913, another major campaign involved:
  • Indian workers.
  • Women.
  • Miners.
  • It protested several discriminatory measures.

37. Indian Women's Role

  • Indian women participated directly in the South African Satyagraha.
  • Kasturba Gandhi was among those imprisoned.

38. Indian Relief Act

  • Negotiations between Gandhi and South African authorities contributed to the Indian Relief Act of 1914.
  • Some major Indian grievances were addressed.

39. Jan Smuts

  • General Jan Smuts was Gandhi's principal South African political opponent and negotiating counterpart during important phases of the struggle.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi in South Africa → Jan Smuts

40. South African Legacy

South Africa gave Gandhi experience in:

  • Mass organisation.
  • Negotiation.
  • Satyagraha.
  • Communal unity.
  • Political journalism.
  • Ashram-based discipline.

41. Departure from South Africa

  • Gandhi left South Africa in 1914.
  • He returned permanently to India in January 1915.

42. Return to India

  • Gandhi arrived in India on 9 January 1915.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi Returned to India → 9 January 1915

43. Pravasi Bharatiya Divas

  • 9 January is observed in India as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, commemorating Gandhi's return from South Africa.

44. Political Mentor

  • Gopal Krishna Gokhale was Gandhi's most important political mentor in India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi's Political Mentor → Gopal Krishna Gokhale

45. Gokhale's Advice

  • Gokhale advised Gandhi to travel throughout India and understand the country before taking a major political role.

46. India Tour

  • Gandhi spent considerable time observing:
  • Rural poverty.
  • Social conditions.
  • Political issues.

before emerging as a national leader.

47. Kochrab Ashram

  • Gandhi established an ashram at Kochrab near Ahmedabad in 1915.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Gandhi Ashram in India → Kochrab → 1915

48. Sabarmati Ashram

  • The ashram was moved to the Sabarmati area in 1917.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sabarmati Ashram → Ahmedabad

49. Sabarmati River

  • Sabarmati Ashram stood on the banks of the Sabarmati River.

50. Ashram Principles

Ashram life emphasised:

  • Truth.
  • Non-violence.
  • Simplicity.
  • Manual labour.
  • Communal living.
  • Self-discipline.

51. Banaras Hindu University Speech

  • Gandhi delivered a significant speech at the opening of Banaras Hindu University in 1916.
  • He criticised:
  • Elite ostentation.
  • Poverty.
  • Distance between political elites and ordinary people.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

BHU Speech → Gandhi → 1916

52. Champaran Satyagraha

  • Gandhi's first major Satyagraha in India took place at Champaran in Bihar in 1917.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Major Gandhi Satyagraha in India → Champaran → 1917

53. Champaran Issue

  • Indigo cultivators were compelled under the Tinkathia system to devote part of their land to indigo cultivation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Champaran → Indigo → Tinkathia

54. Raj Kumar Shukla

  • Peasant Raj Kumar Shukla persuaded Gandhi to visit Champaran.
📌 Must-Memorise

Raj Kumar Shukla → Brought Gandhi to Champaran

55. Gandhi's Investigation

  • Gandhi and his associates collected testimonies from cultivators regarding planter exploitation.

56. Civil Disobedience at Champaran

  • Gandhi refused an official order directing him to leave the district.
  • He accepted legal consequences rather than obey what he considered an unjust command.

57. Champaran Associates

Important associates included:

  • Rajendra Prasad.
  • J.B. Kripalani.
  • Brajkishore Prasad.
  • Mazharul Haq.

58. Result of Champaran

  • An inquiry committee was appointed.
  • The oppressive indigo arrangement was progressively dismantled.

59. Importance of Champaran

Champaran demonstrated:

  • Satyagraha in Indian conditions.
  • Peasant mobilisation.
  • Gandhi's growing national leadership.

60. Ahmedabad Mill Strike

  • Gandhi intervened in a dispute between textile workers and mill owners at Ahmedabad in 1918.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ahmedabad → Mill Workers → 1918

61. Anasuya Sarabhai

  • Anasuya Sarabhai was an important labour organiser associated with the Ahmedabad struggle.
📌 Must-Memorise

Anasuya Sarabhai → Ahmedabad Labour Movement

62. Gandhi's Fast

  • Gandhi undertook a fast during the Ahmedabad labour dispute.
  • The strike ended through negotiated settlement.

63. Kheda Satyagraha

  • Kheda Satyagraha occurred in Gujarat in 1918.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kheda → Peasants → 1918

64. Cause of Kheda Movement

  • Crop failure made it difficult for peasants to pay land revenue.
  • They demanded suspension or remission of revenue.

65. Vallabhbhai Patel

  • Vallabhbhai Patel emerged as an important organiser during the Kheda campaign.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kheda → Gandhi + Vallabhbhai Patel

66. Three Early Gandhi Movements

  • Champaran → 1917 → Indigo cultivators.
  • Ahmedabad → 1918 → Mill workers.
  • Kheda → 1918 → Peasants.
📌 Must-Memorise

Champaran → Peasant

Ahmedabad → Labour

Kheda → Revenue

67. Gandhi's Leadership Expansion

These struggles established Gandhi as a leader who could connect with:

  • Peasants.
  • Workers.
  • Local activists.

68. Rowlatt Act

  • The Rowlatt Act was passed in 1919.
  • It extended extraordinary powers of detention and repression.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rowlatt Act → 1919

69. Rowlatt Satyagraha

  • Gandhi launched an all-India Satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Gandhi All-India Satyagraha → Rowlatt → 1919

70. Satyagraha Sabha

  • Gandhi organised a Satyagraha Sabha to coordinate opposition.

71. Hartal

  • Gandhi called for a nationwide hartal in April 1919.
  • Demonstrations occurred across many cities.

72. Violence and Gandhi

  • Violence broke out in some areas.
  • Gandhi suspended the campaign and later described the premature mass mobilisation as a serious mistake.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gandhi → Non-Violence Was a Condition of Satyagraha

73. Jallianwala Bagh Massacre

  • The massacre occurred at Amritsar on 13 April 1919.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jallianwala Bagh → 13 April 1919

74. General Dyer

  • Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered soldiers to fire on the unarmed gathering.

75. Impact on Gandhi

  • Jallianwala Bagh and broader Punjab repression weakened Gandhi's remaining faith in the moral legitimacy of British rule.

76. Kaiser-i-Hind Medal

  • Gandhi had previously received the Kaiser-i-Hind medal for public service.
  • He returned British honours during the Non-Cooperation phase in protest against colonial policies.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gandhi → Returned British Honours

77. Khilafat Movement

  • Gandhi supported the Khilafat Movement after the First World War.
  • He saw Hindu-Muslim cooperation as essential to national struggle.

78. Ali Brothers

Important Khilafat leaders included:

  • Mohammad Ali.
  • Shaukat Ali.

79. Maulana Abul Kalam Azad

  • Maulana Azad also became an important leader of anti-colonial Muslim politics and Congress nationalism.

80. Gandhi and Khilafat

  • Gandhi connected Khilafat grievances with the wider Non-Cooperation programme.

81. Non-Cooperation Movement

  • Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920.
📌 Must-Memorise

Non-Cooperation Movement → 1920–1922

82. Calcutta Special Session

  • The Congress accepted the Non-Cooperation programme at its special Calcutta session in September 1920.

83. Nagpur Congress

  • The programme was ratified and Congress reorganised at Nagpur in December 1920.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nagpur 1920 → Congress Mass Reorganisation

84. Non-Cooperation Programme

It included:

  • Surrender of titles.
  • Boycott of government schools.
  • Boycott of law courts.
  • Boycott of legislative councils.
  • Boycott of foreign cloth.
  • Promotion of khadi.

85. Lawyers Leaving Practice

Some nationalist lawyers gave up or reduced legal practice as part of Non-Cooperation.

86. Students

  • Students withdrew from government-controlled institutions in several regions.
  • National educational institutions were established.

87. Khadi

  • Gandhi made khadi a central symbol of:
  • Swadeshi.
  • Self-reliance.
  • Rural employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khadi → Gandhi → Swadeshi + Self-Reliance

88. Charkha

  • The spinning wheel became a major Gandhian political and economic symbol.
📌 Must-Memorise

Charkha → Gandhian Constructive Programme

89. Foreign Cloth Boycott

  • Public burning and boycott of foreign cloth became a visible form of nationalist protest.

90. Mass Expansion

Non-Cooperation brought into politics:

  • Peasants.
  • Workers.
  • Traders.
  • Students.
  • Women.
  • Religious leaders.

91. Chauri Chaura

  • Chauri Chaura incident occurred in Gorakhpur district on 5 February 1922.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chauri Chaura → 5 February 1922

92. Chauri Chaura Violence

  • Protesters attacked and burned a police station.
  • More than twenty policemen were killed.

93. Withdrawal of Non-Cooperation

  • Gandhi suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement after the Chauri Chaura violence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chauri Chaura → Gandhi Withdrew Non-Cooperation

94. Reason for Withdrawal

  • Gandhi believed political freedom gained through uncontrolled violence would contradict Satyagraha.

95. Criticism of Withdrawal

  • Several nationalist leaders were disappointed by the sudden suspension.
  • The episode demonstrated major strategic differences within the movement.

96. Gandhi Arrested

  • Gandhi was arrested in March 1922 on charges of sedition.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi Imprisoned → 1922

97. Trial

  • Gandhi accepted responsibility for his writings and defended resistance to unjust rule.

98. Six-Year Sentence

  • He was sentenced to six years' imprisonment.
  • He was released early in 1924 because of health problems.

99. Belgaum Congress

  • Gandhi presided over the Indian National Congress session at Belgaum in 1924.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi's Only INC Presidency → Belgaum → 1924

100. Communal Harmony Fast

  • Gandhi undertook a 21-day fast in 1924 in an effort to promote Hindu-Muslim unity.

101. Constructive Programme

After Non-Cooperation, Gandhi placed greater emphasis on:

  • Khadi.
  • Village industries.
  • Hindu-Muslim unity.
  • Removal of untouchability.
  • Sanitation.
  • Basic education.

102. All India Spinners' Association

  • Gandhi established the All India Spinners' Association in 1925.
📌 Must-Memorise

All India Spinners' Association → 1925

103. Swaraj

For Gandhi, Swaraj included:

  • Political self-rule.
  • Individual self-discipline.
  • Village self-government.
  • Social reform.

104. Hind Swaraj

  • Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj in 1909.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hind Swaraj → Gandhi → 1909

105. Original Language

  • Hind Swaraj was originally written in Gujarati.

106. Hind Swaraj — Main Ideas

It criticised aspects of:

  • Modern industrial civilisation.
  • Materialism.
  • Violent nationalism.
  • Colonial dependence.

107. Gandhi's Autobiography

  • Gandhi wrote The Story of My Experiments with Truth.
📌 Must-Memorise

My Experiments with Truth → Gandhi

108. Original Gujarati Title

  • Gandhi's autobiography was originally written in Gujarati.
  • It was serialised during the 1920s.

109. Mahadev Desai

  • Mahadev Desai was Gandhi's close secretary and associate.
  • He translated Gandhi's autobiography into English.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahadev Desai → Gandhi's Secretary

110. Young India

  • Gandhi edited the English-language journal Young India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Young India → Gandhi

111. Navajivan

  • Gandhi also edited Navajivan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Navajivan → Gandhi

112. Harijan

  • Gandhi later published the weekly Harijan to promote social reform and opposition to untouchability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harijan → Gandhi's Anti-Untouchability Journalism

113. Simon Commission

  • Gandhi and Congress opposed the Simon Commission because it contained no Indian member.

114. Bardoli

  • Gandhi supported the Bardoli movement of 1928 led by Vallabhbhai Patel.
  • The success greatly strengthened Patel's national reputation.

115. Lahore Congress

  • At Lahore in December 1929, Congress adopted Purna Swaraj under Jawaharlal Nehru's presidency.

116. Independence Day

  • Congress observed 26 January 1930 as Independence Day.
📌 Must-Memorise

26 January 1930 → Purna Swaraj Independence Day

117. Civil Disobedience Movement

  • Gandhi launched the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930.
📌 Must-Memorise

Civil Disobedience → 1930

118. Why Salt?

Gandhi chose salt because:

  • Everyone used it.
  • The tax affected rich and poor.
  • Government monopoly symbolised colonial control.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Salt → Universal Mass Issue

119. Letter to Lord Irwin

  • Before beginning the Salt March, Gandhi wrote to Viceroy Lord Irwin outlining major grievances and demands.

120. Dandi March

  • Gandhi began the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram on 12 March 1930.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dandi March Begins → 12 March 1930

121. Initial Marchers

  • Gandhi began the march with 78 selected Satyagrahis.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dandi March → Gandhi + 78 Initial Satyagrahis

122. Route

  • The march travelled from Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal village of Dandi in Gujarat.

123. Distance

  • The march covered roughly 390 kilometres, or around 240 miles.

124. Arrival at Dandi

  • Gandhi reached Dandi on 5 April 1930.

125. Breaking the Salt Law

  • On 6 April 1930, Gandhi broke the colonial salt law by making or collecting salt.
📌 Must-Memorise

Salt Law Broken → Dandi → 6 April 1930

126. Nationwide Civil Disobedience

The movement spread through:

  • Salt making.
  • Tax resistance.
  • Forest-law violations.
  • Foreign-cloth boycott.
  • Picketing.

127. Women's Participation

Women participated widely in:

  • Salt making.
  • Picketing.
  • Processions.
  • Boycotts.

128. Sarojini Naidu

  • Sarojini Naidu became a major leader during the Salt Satyagraha phase.

129. Dharasana Salt Works

  • After Gandhi's arrest, Satyagrahis continued resistance at Dharasana Salt Works.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dharasana → Salt Satyagraha

130. Abbas Tyabji

  • Abbas Tyabji initially assumed leadership of the planned Dharasana action after Gandhi's arrest.

131. Sarojini Naidu at Dharasana

  • After further arrests, Sarojini Naidu became a prominent leader of the Dharasana campaign.

132. Gandhi Arrested — 1930

  • Gandhi was arrested in May 1930 during the Civil Disobedience Movement.

133. International Attention

  • Reports of non-violent protesters being beaten drew international attention to British repression.

134. Tamil Nadu — Vedaranyam Salt March

  • C. Rajagopalachari led the Tamil Nadu Salt Satyagraha from Tiruchirappalli to Vedaranyam in April 1930.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha → Rajaji → 1930

135. Vedaranyam Significance

  • It was the major Tamil Nadu parallel to Gandhi's Dandi March.

136. Gandhi–Irwin Pact

  • Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin concluded the Gandhi–Irwin Pact on 5 March 1931.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi–Irwin Pact → 5 March 1931

137. Main Terms

Broadly:

  • Congress suspended Civil Disobedience.
  • Government agreed to release many non-violent political prisoners.
  • Peaceful picketing was permitted.
  • Limited manufacture of salt in coastal areas was allowed.

138. Karachi Congress

  • Congress ratified the Gandhi–Irwin Pact at Karachi in 1931.
  • Vallabhbhai Patel presided.

139. Second Round Table Conference

  • Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in London in 1931.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi → Second Round Table Conference → 1931

140. Congress Representation

  • Gandhi attended as the sole official representative of the Indian National Congress.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Congress at Second RTC → Gandhi

141. Main Issues at RTC

Discussions included:

  • Constitutional structure.
  • Federalism.
  • Minority representation.
  • Communal representation.

142. Failure of Second RTC

  • The conference failed to produce an agreement acceptable to Congress.
  • Gandhi returned to India disappointed.

143. Civil Disobedience Resumed

  • Gandhi resumed Civil Disobedience after returning to India.
  • He was arrested again in January 1932.

144. Yerwada Jail

  • Gandhi was imprisoned at Yerwada Central Jail in Pune.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi 1932 → Yerwada Jail

145. Communal Award

  • British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award in August 1932.

146. Separate Electorates for Depressed Classes

  • The Award proposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.
  • Gandhi opposed this provision.

147. Gandhi's Fast

  • Gandhi began a fast in Yerwada Jail on 20 September 1932.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi's Poona Pact Fast → 20 September 1932

148. B.R. Ambedkar

  • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the leading political representative demanding effective safeguards for the Depressed Classes.

149. Poona Pact

  • The Poona Pact was concluded on 24 September 1932.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poona Pact → 24 September 1932

150. Poona Pact Formula

It replaced:

  • Separate electorates.

with:

  • Joint electorates.
  • Reserved seats for Depressed Classes.

151. Gandhi–Ambedkar Difference

They both opposed untouchability but differed sharply on:

  • Nature of caste.
  • Representation.
  • Political safeguards.
  • Strategy of social reform.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Gandhi and Ambedkar → Shared Opposition to Untouchability, Different Approaches

152. Anti-Untouchability Campaign

  • After the Poona Pact, Gandhi greatly intensified his campaign against untouchability.

153. Harijan Sevak Sangh

  • The All India Anti-Untouchability League was established in 1932 and soon became known as the Harijan Sevak Sangh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harijan Sevak Sangh → Anti-Untouchability Organisation

154. "Harijan"

  • Gandhi used the term Harijan for people subjected to untouchability.
  • The term later came to be rejected by many Dalit thinkers and organisations.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Use Modern Constitutional Term → Scheduled Castes

Historical Gandhi Usage → Harijan

155. Harijan Tours

  • Gandhi toured extensively to raise funds and public support for the removal of untouchability.

156. Temple Entry

  • Gandhi supported campaigns for opening temples and public facilities to communities excluded by untouchability.

157. Vaikom Satyagraha

  • Vaikom Satyagraha of 1924–25 challenged caste-based restrictions around the Vaikom temple in Travancore.
  • Gandhi visited Vaikom and participated in negotiations.
🔗 South India Key Link

Vaikom → Anti-Untouchability Movement

158. Periyar at Vaikom

  • E.V. Ramasamy participated prominently in the Vaikom struggle.
  • His approach to caste later differed significantly from Gandhi's.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Vaikom → Gandhi + Periyar in Different Roles

159. Temple Entry Proclamation

  • The Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation was issued in 1936.
  • It opened temples under Travancore state control to previously excluded Hindu communities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation → 1936

160. Gandhi Leaves Congress Organisation

  • In 1934 Gandhi withdrew from formal Congress membership to focus more on constructive work.
  • He nevertheless remained the movement's dominant moral and political influence.

161. Village Industries

  • Gandhi promoted revival of village industries to:
  • Reduce rural unemployment.
  • Encourage self-reliance.
  • Limit dependence on imported goods.

162. All India Village Industries Association

  • Gandhian constructive workers developed institutions for promoting village industries during the 1930s.
  • J.C. Kumarappa became a major Gandhian economist associated with this work.
📌 Must-Memorise

J.C. Kumarappa → Gandhian Economics

163. J.C. Kumarappa

  • Joseph Cornelius Kumarappa was a Tamil-origin economist and important interpreter of Gandhian economic ideas.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

J.C. Kumarappa → Gandhian Economist

164. Gandhian Economics

Major ideas included:

  • Decentralisation.
  • Village industries.
  • Limitation of excessive consumption.
  • Local self-reliance.
  • Ethical economics.

165. Trusteeship

  • Gandhi developed the concept of Trusteeship.
  • Wealth holders were expected to treat property as a trust for wider social welfare.
📌 Must-Memorise

Trusteeship → Gandhi

166. Private Property — Gandhi's Position

  • Gandhi did not simply advocate unrestricted capitalism.
  • He sought moral and social responsibility in the use of wealth.

167. Gram Swaraj

  • Gandhi envisioned self-reliant and politically empowered villages as foundations of Indian democracy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gram Swaraj → Gandhi

168. Panchayats

  • Gandhi regarded local self-government as essential to genuine Swaraj.

169. Nai Talim

  • Gandhi promoted Basic Education, commonly known as Nai Talim.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nai Talim → Gandhian Basic Education

170. Wardha Scheme of Education

  • A major conference on Gandhian basic education was held at Wardha in 1937.
📌 Must-Memorise

Wardha Scheme → 1937

171. Zakir Husain Committee

  • A committee chaired by Dr. Zakir Husain developed the detailed scheme of Basic Education.
📌 Must-Memorise

Basic Education Committee → Zakir Husain

172. Basic Education Principle

Education should integrate:

  • Productive craft.
  • Intellectual learning.

What is Nai Talim? → Gandhian Basic Education.

Which educational scheme is associated with Wardha? → Basic Education Scheme, 1937.

Who chaired the committee that developed it? → Dr. Zakir Husain.

Where was Gandhi's later principal ashram? → Sevagram near Wardha.

When did Individual Satyagraha begin? → 1940.

Who was the first Individual Satyagrahi? → Vinoba Bhave.

Who was the second prominent Satyagrahi? → Jawaharlal Nehru.

When did Cripps Mission come to India? → 1942.

Which movement followed its failure? → Quit India Movement.

When was Quit India Resolution adopted? → 8 August 1942.

Where? → Bombay.

Which venue? → Gowalia Tank Maidan.

What is its present name? → August Kranti Maidan.

What famous slogan did Gandhi give? → Do or Die.

When was Gandhi arrested? → 9 August 1942.

Where was Gandhi detained? → Aga Khan Palace, Pune.

Who died there in August 1942? → Mahadev Desai.

Who died there on 22 February 1944? → Kasturba Gandhi.

When was Gandhi released? → May 1944.

With whom did Gandhi hold talks in 1944? → Muhammad Ali Jinnah.

Which Tamil leader's formula influenced these negotiations? → C. Rajagopalachari.

Which Bengal district became central to Gandhi's peace mission in 1946? → Noakhali.

Where was Gandhi on 15 August 1947? → Calcutta, working for communal peace.

When did Gandhi begin his final fast? → 13 January 1948.

When did it end? → 18 January 1948.

When was Gandhi assassinated? → 30 January 1948.

Who assassinated him? → Nathuram Godse.

Where? → Birla House, New Delhi.

What is Gandhi's principal memorial in Delhi? → Raj Ghat.

Which day is observed as Martyrs' Day? → 30 January.

Who addressed Gandhi as "Father of our Nation" in 1944? → Subhas Chandra Bose.

What was Gandhi affectionately called? → Bapu.

Who helped popularise the title Mahatma for Gandhi? → Rabindranath Tagore, though claims about the exact first use are disputed.

Which Tamil city is associated with Gandhi's decision to adopt simpler dress? → Madurai.

When? → September 1921.

What did his simple dress symbolise? → Identification with India's poor, khadi and Swadeshi.

Who was the major Gandhian economist with a Tamil connection? → J.C. Kumarappa.

What does Ahimsa mean in Gandhi's philosophy? → Non-violence combined with absence of hatred.

What is the relationship between means and ends in Gandhian thought? → Good ends require morally defensible means.

What did Gandhi mean by Ram Rajya? → Ethical and just government, not a Hindu theocracy.

What was Gandhi's preferred economic emphasis? → Decentralisation, village industries and self-reliance.

What were the Seven Social Sins popularised by Gandhi? → Politics without principle; wealth without work; pleasure without conscience; knowledge without character; commerce without morality; science without humanity; worship without sacrifice.

Which five major Gandhian centres should be remembered? → Phoenix Settlement, Tolstoy Farm, Kochrab Ashram, Sabarmati Ashram and Sevagram.

Did Gandhi ever receive the Nobel Peace Prize? → No.

What is observed internationally on Gandhi's birthday? → International Day of Non-Violence.

What is the core TNPSC takeaway? → Gandhi transformed India's freedom struggle into a mass movement through Satyagraha, Ahimsa, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, constructive work and Quit India while linking political independence with social and moral reform.
